options.text: Data is collected from part of the population.
Data is collected from every member of the population.
options.why: This describes a census — collecting from everyone is exactly what a sample does not do.

options.text: Data is collected whenever the population has more than one thousand members.
options.why: Uses the size of the population as the deciding feature, when what matters is that only part of it was included.

options.text: Data is collected from every member of a small population.
options.why: Still describes a census, with an extra size condition that plays no part in the definition.

questions.solution_text:
A census collects data from the whole population.
A sample collects data from only some of it.
**Data is collected from part of the population.**

questions.question_text:
A scanner on a biscuit factory line checks every packet that leaves the line for a missing label.
Is this a census or a sample of the packets produced?

options.text: A census, because every packet produced is checked.
A sample, because only the packets that leave the line are checked.
options.why: Assumes some packets are missed, but every packet produced leaves the line, so none are left out.

options.text: A sample, because a machine and not a person collects the data.
options.why: Confuses who collects the data with how much of the population is covered; an automatic check can still cover everyone.

options.text: A sample, because the packets are checked one at a time.
options.why: Checking items one at a time is still a census when every item is eventually checked.

questions.solution_text:
The population is every packet produced on the line.
The scanner checks all of them.
**A census.**

questions.question_text:
Rangers estimate the number of fish in a lake by netting, tagging and releasing $150$ fish.
Is this a census or a sample of the fish in the lake?

options.text: A sample, because only $150$ of the lake's fish are handled.
A census, because every fish that was netted is tagged.
options.why: Treats the netted group as the population; the population is all the fish in the lake, not only the ones caught.

options.text: A census, because the rangers are investigating the whole lake.
options.why: Confuses covering the whole lake as a place with covering every fish in it.

options.text: A census, because $150$ fish is a large number to handle.
options.why: Uses the size of the group collected instead of asking whether every fish in the lake was included.

questions.solution_text:
The population is all the fish in the lake.
Only $150$ of them are netted and tagged.
**A sample.**

questions.question_text:
A school of $1200$ students wants to know what all of its students think of the new timetable.
The SRC surveys the $30$ students in the school band.
What is the population being investigated?

options.text: All $1200$ students at the school.
The $30$ students in the school band.
options.why: Names the sample rather than the population; the band members are the part that happened to be surveyed.

options.text: The members of the SRC who ran the survey.
options.why: Names the people collecting the data instead of the group being investigated.

options.text: All students and all teachers at the school.
options.why: Widens the population beyond the group the school asked about, which was its students.

questions.solution_text:
The population is every individual the school wants information about.
The school wants to know what all of its students think.
**All $1200$ students at the school.**

questions.question_text:
A tyre manufacturer measures how far a tyre travels before it wears out by running tyres until they are destroyed.
Why must the manufacturer use a sample rather than a census?

options.text: Testing destroys the tyre, so a census would leave no tyres to sell.
Every tyre is identical, so testing more than one would tell them nothing new.
options.why: Assumes the items are identical; a sample is needed here because the test is destructive, not because tyres never vary.

options.text: A sample gives a more accurate result than a census does.
options.why: Reverses the accuracy: a census gives the exact result and a sample only estimates it.

options.text: The population of tyres is too small for a census to be possible.
options.why: A small population makes a census easier rather than impossible; it is the destruction of each tested tyre that rules it out.

questions.solution_text:
Each tyre tested is worn out and cannot be sold.
A census would mean destroying every tyre made.
**Testing destroys the tyre, so only a sample can be tested.**

questions.question_text:
Every enrolled voter in a country votes in a referendum on changing the constitution.
Is this a census or a sample of enrolled voters?

options.text: A census, because every enrolled voter takes part.
A sample, because millions of voters is far too many to be everyone.
options.why: Assumes a very large population rules out a census; a census can cover millions as long as no one is left out.

options.text: A sample, because some voters will fill in their ballot incorrectly.
options.why: Confuses spoiled ballots with who was included; the collection still reaches every enrolled voter.

options.text: A sample, because only enrolled voters take part and not the whole country.
options.why: The stated population is enrolled voters, so covering all of them is a census of that population.

questions.solution_text:
The population is every enrolled voter.
All of them take part in the referendum.
**A census.**

questions.question_text:
A drama teacher needs the height of each of the $18$ students in her class so she can order costumes.
Which method is more appropriate, and why?

options.text: A census, because the population is small and it gives every student's exact height.
A sample, because measuring all $18$ students would take far too long.
options.why: Overstates the cost of a census of $18$ people; time only rules out a census for very large populations.

options.text: A sample, because measuring a few students is enough to estimate the rest.
options.why: An estimate is useless here — each costume has to fit the student it is ordered for.

options.text: A sample, because a census is only possible for a population under ten.
options.why: Invents a size limit on a census; a census simply means including everyone, whatever the population size.

questions.solution_text:
The population is the $18$ students in the class.
Measuring all $18$ is quick and gives each student's exact height.
**A census.**

questions.question_text:
A council counts every one of the $240$ trees in Miller Park.
The council's report is about the health of the trees across the whole council area, which has about $9000$ trees.
For the council's investigation, is the count a census or a sample?

options.text: A sample, because the population is all $9000$ trees in the council area.
A census, because every tree in Miller Park was counted.
options.why: Uses the park as the population; the report's population is the whole council area, so the park trees are only part of it.

options.text: A census, because the council collected all of the data itself.
options.why: Confuses who collected the data with how much of the population it covers.

options.text: A sample, because only some of the trees in Miller Park were healthy.
options.why: Bases the label on the results found rather than on how much of the population was included.

questions.solution_text:
The population for this report is all $9000$ trees in the council area.
Only the $240$ trees in Miller Park were counted.
**A sample.**
